Introduction
This annotated bibliography evaluates sources that informed my case study on the conservative
management of knee osteoarthritis, with attention to their credibility, relevance and limitations
for practice in primary care settings.
Annotated Bibliography
Brophy, Robert H., and Yale A. Fillingham. "AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline Summary:
Management of Osteoarthritis of the Knee." Journal of the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, vol. 30, no. 9, 2022, pp. e721–29.
This guideline summary presents the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons'
recommendations for managing knee osteoarthritis without joint replacement. The authors
grade each intervention by strength of evidence and conclude that supervised exercise, weight
loss and patient education should form the foundation of care, while several popular injections
lack convincing support.
The source is highly credible because it was produced by a professional body through a
systematic review process. I will use it to justify the conservative management plan in my case
study, particularly the decision to postpone imaging until the exercise programme has been
tried.
Elliott, Anthony. The Routledge Companion to Social Theory. Routledge, 2010.
The authors update the European recommendations for non-pharmacological management of
hip and knee osteoarthritis. They argue that exercise, education and weight management should
be offered to every patient, and they emphasise shared decision making and regular review of
goals.
Although the recommendations are thorough, they were developed mainly for European health
systems, so some service models may not transfer directly to primary care in other countries.
Nevertheless, the article strengthens my argument that education must accompany every
exercise prescription.
Porter, Louise. Young Children's Behaviour: Guidance Approaches for Early Childhood
Educators. 4th ed., Allen & Unwin, 2016.
Porter explains how educators can guide young children's behaviour by meeting their needs
rather than controlling them. She contrasts authoritarian discipline with guidance approaches
and shows how communication, listening and self-regulation support lasting change in
children's behaviour.
This book is useful for my reflection because it gave me language to analyse the trampoline
incident I observed. Its limitation is that it is written for early childhood settings, so I must be
careful when applying its ideas to older learners.

Smith, Melissa H., and Jessica R. Berman. "What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?" JAMA, vol. 327, no.
12, 2022, p. 1194.
This fact sheet summarises the global burden of musculoskeletal conditions and explains why
they are the leading cause of disability worldwide. It highlights low back pain and osteoarthritis
as the largest contributors and calls for rehabilitation to be integrated into primary health care.
The source is authoritative but brief, so I will use it only to establish the scale of the problem in
my introduction rather than to support specific clinical decisions.
